..
KEY MESSAGE 1...

Despite weak upper-level forcing, ample warmth and moisture 
surging into the region along the northwest periphery of a 
Bermuda High will be sufficient to drive surface-based forcing
for ascent for the initiation of scattered to numerous showers 
and thunderstorms across the region today. In fact, the
combination of high temperatures widely reaching the mid to
upper 80s and dewpoints the low to mid 70s will see SBCAPE
values reach 2000-3000 J/kg by this afternoon. This appreciable
instability, paired with deep layer shear on the order of 
20-35 kt and meager mid- level lapse rates (generally < 6 C/km)
yield the low, though non-zero probability (~5-10% severe
thunderstorms) of isolated severe- level convection this 
afternoon. Therefore, the Storm Prediction Center has not only 
maintained, but expanded, the Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) for 
Severe Weather across most of our area. The primary threat for 
any storm that reaches severe strength will be locally damaging 
wind gusts. However, should breaks in cloud cover not occur as 
some of the guidance suggests, it could be difficult for storms 
to grow tall enough to reach severe strength. Additionally, some
of the latest CAMs are showing subtle low- to mid-level capping
inversions which could also act to inhibit storm growth. 

That said, even if developing showers/storms this afternoon 
don't evolve into severe-level convection, any shower or non-
severe thunderstorm will be capable of producing gusty winds and
moderate to heavy rainfall. The "ample moisture" mentioned
previously can be classified more accurately as above-normal
atmospheric moisture content for this time of year given PWAT
values achieve +2 STDEVs (~ 2-2.2" across our CWA). Warm and
efficient precipitation processes paired with high instability
will support frequent moderate to heavy downpours this 
afternoon. And, with fairly slow storm motion, potential for 
training convection, and wet antecedent conditions, isolated 
flash flooding cannot be ruled out. The Weather Prediction
Center has therefore outlined our entire area in a Marginal Risk
(Level 1 of 4) for Excessive Rainfall. Likewise, precipitation 
loading will promote rapid downward acceleration (DCAPE values 
~500-700 J/kg) and resulting gusty winds associated with showers
and thunderstorms.

Friday, though the environment will be similar, is a little more
uncertain than today. HiRes guidance is highly varied, given 
the short lead time, regarding the coverage of another potential
round of showers and thunderstorms. While some model solutions
point to very limited coverage of convection, others have more
robust storms than what is projected for today. The thinking
behind this is that some of the guidance is erring towards more
convection today, which could stabilize the environment
sufficiently to inhibit convection tomorrow, while others are 
resolving a potential remnant MCV that tracks through the Ohio
Valley and drives stronger convection here tomorrow. With
another hot, humid day anticipated tomorrow with slightly more
upper-level forcing given an approaching shortwave, the latter
is certainly possible. In fact, the latest REFS continues to
show low probabilities (~5-14%) for severe-level wind gusts for
Friday. We will continue to monitor trends in the guidance to
iron out the coverage details. But as of right now, the Storm
Prediction Center has maintained a Marginal Risk just to our 
south for Friday. The Weather Prediction Center, too, has 
maintained a Marginal Risk for Excessive Rainfall given the 
persistent potential for heavy rainfall within any showers and 
storms that may develop. 

Additional showers and thunderstorms are expected heading into
the beginning of the weekend as the system partially 
responsible for our convection today and possibly tomorrow 
finally starts to shift into the region from the northwest. We
will continue to have the potential for moderate to heavy
downpours with gusty winds within these showers and storms so
for the third day in a row, we will remain in a Marginal Risk 
for Excessive Rainfall. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Today and tomorrow will be very warm and humid given our
position relative to the Bermuda High to our southeast. High
temperatures both days will widely reach the mid to upper 80s
with dewpoints in the low to mid 70s in valley areas. That said,
the most uncomfortable areas will be portions of the lower Mid-
Hudson Valley (eastern Ulster and western Dutchess Counties) and
southern Litchfield County where a Heat Advisory remains in 
effect from 11 AM today through 8 PM Friday. Here, heat index
values, or feels-like temperatures, will reach up to 98 degrees
Fahrenheit. Caution is advised particularly to those who are
susceptible to heat-related illness.
